stages.name: Government failure
stages.title: Government failure
stages.sub: Why government intervention can sometimes make a market worse off, and the main reasons this happens.

steps.q: A government caps rent to help tenants, but landlords withdraw flats and the shortage worsens. Has the intervention definitely made things better?
steps.right: No, it could leave society worse off
steps.hint: Think about what happened to the total supply of homes after the cap.
steps.pre: When intervention ends up causing a net loss of welfare, that is

steps.q: A subsidy makes wheat far cheaper than it costs to grow. Do farmers now know what wheat is worth to buyers?
steps.right: No, the price no longer reflects true value
steps.wrong: Yes, the price still shows true value
steps.hint: Prices normally tell producers what buyers value. What happens to that message once it is propped up artificially?

steps.q: A sugary drinks tax is meant to cut sugar, but people switch to sugary snacks. Did it only produce its intended effect?
steps.right: No, it also caused side effects nobody planned
steps.wrong: Yes, it worked exactly as intended
steps.hint: Compare the goal of the tax with what people actually did in response.

steps.q: A subsidy scheme's inspectors, forms and staff eat much of the money meant for farmers. Does every pound reach them?
steps.right: No, a lot is spent just running the scheme
steps.wrong: Yes, it all reaches the people intended
steps.hint: Think about the staff and paperwork needed to operate the scheme, separate from the actual payments.

steps.q: A government sets a pollution limit from outdated data, not knowing how firms will react. Can it be sure it's right?
steps.right: No, it is guessing without full knowledge
steps.wrong: Yes, it can calculate the exact right limit
steps.hint: Does the government have complete, accurate knowledge of every firm's behaviour before it sets the rule?
